notes: Ancillary relief farming case; inherited property and White v White principles are clearly analysed in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Divorce ancillary relief where farm was husband's inherited property
key_facts: Mr and Mrs P divorced after a 19-year marriage during which they farmed a hill farm in the husband's family for four generations.
Agreed net family assets were about £2.5 million, overwhelmingly represented by inherited farmland and related assets held mainly in the husband's sole name.
The wife moved south with two children needing private school fees and sought up to 40% of assets or alternatively housing plus a Duxbury fund.
The husband sought to retain the farm in specie and proposed a lump sum of £340,000 for housing only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Ancillary relief application following decree nisi in divorce proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Wife awarded lump sum of £575,000 (£400,000 housing and £175,000 capitalised income), plus child maintenance and school fees orders; percentage-based division rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Where the bulk of matrimonial assets represent a multi-generational inherited farm brought into the marriage to be retained in specie, fairness may require a needs-based award rather than percentage division under White v White; inherited property is a section 25 factor whose weight depends on nature, value and circumstances, but the claimant's reasonable needs must still be met and cannot be capped by the paying party's free capital alone.
legal_issues: Whether a percentage-based division under White v White was appropriate
How to treat inherited farmland within section 25 Matrimonial Causes Act 1973
Whether the wife's claim should be limited to reasonable needs
Whether sale of the farm was required to meet the wife's award

notes: Lease consent to alterations dispute at Whittlebury Hall; reasonableness of use-restriction condition is fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Reasonableness of landlord condition restricting hotel extension use
key_facts: Macepark held a long lease of Whittlebury Hall hotel near Silverstone and sought consent to a major extension with bedrooms and conference facilities.
Landlords Mr and Mrs Sargeant also operated competing wedding and functions businesses on adjoining land.
The parties settled on a licence leaving one issue: whether a covenant restricting public rooms to management-training-related functions was a reasonable condition of consent.
Macepark had begun works without consent, leading to interim injunction proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issue following settlement, on whether a proposed lease variation condition was reasonable.
enrichment.outcome: Condition held unreasonable as drafted; lease not varied to incorporate clause 3.34 restricting extension use to management training conferences only.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord may impose a reasonable condition protecting legitimate concerns about competitive use of altered premises, including trading interests in adjoining property, but an absolute restriction limiting public rooms to management training conferences only went further than reasonably necessary where it would exclude much of the tenant's existing permitted conference business.
legal_issues: Whether consent to alterations had been unreasonably withheld or delayed
Whether a landlord may refuse consent or impose conditions to protect trading interests in adjoining land
Application of International Drilling Fluids and Iqbal principles to alterations covenants
Whether section 19(2) Landlord and Tenant Act 1927 limited the landlord to seeking compensation only

notes: Interlocutory appeal on fresh evidence after claim amendment in Tenby harbour parking JR; Ladd v Marshall analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Fresh evidence allowed on harbour parking judicial review appeal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Richards challenged Pembrokeshire County Council parking regulations affecting a raised terrace near Tenby Harbour.
At trial they amended to argue the regulations were ultra vires because the terrace was not harbour land and not for harbour operational purposes.
The council sought to adduce further witness evidence on harbour operational impact after the amendment.
Moses J had permitted the amendment and considered the council not prejudiced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal against a decision allowing further evidence on a pending judicial review appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application to adduce further evidence allowed; Richards given until 3 pm Friday to file responsive evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant amends at trial to raise a new ultra vires argument based on harbour operational purpose rather than geographical scope, it is fair to permit the respondent to adduce further evidence addressing harbour operations even if not strictly within Ladd v Marshall, because the new issue was not reasonably foreseeable before amendment.
legal_issues: Whether additional witness statements should be admitted on appeal
Application of Ladd v Marshall criteria to fresh evidence
Whether the council was prejudiced by a late amendment on harbour operational purpose
Admissibility of evidence explaining the council's decision-making
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489
Hertfordshire Investments Ltd v Bubb [2000] 1 WLR 2318
R v Licensing Authority for Goods Vehicles for the Metropolitan Traffic Area ex p Barrett Ltd [1949] 2 KB 17

notes: Oxford Street pavement trip claim; dangerous defect and section 58 Highways Act defence analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Pavement trip on Oxford Street defeated by section 58 defence
key_facts: A visitor in her 70s tripped on uneven rocking paving stones outside Selfridges on Oxford Street in March 2000.
The gap between stones created a trap of about 15–20mm when the rear stone depressed.
Westminster maintained the pavement through monthly inspections and reactive repairs using a 20mm intervention threshold.
The paving was later filled in after the accident, identified by the claimant's solicitors in 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim in negligence and breach of statutory duty for failure to maintain the highway.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; primary liability made out but section 58 defence established on the basis of reasonable inspection and maintenance systems.
enrichment.ratio: A rocking paving stone creating a foreseeable trip trap may breach the section 1 maintenance duty, but a highway authority escapes liability under section 58 if it proves it took such care as was reasonably required to keep the relevant part of the highway safe, including through reasonable periodic inspection and reactive maintenance systems.
legal_issues: Whether the pavement was dangerous to traffic within the meaning of highway case law
Whether the defect resulted from failure to maintain the highway
Whether Westminster's monthly inspection and 20mm intervention system satisfied section 58
Whether res ipsa loquitur applied
linked_authorities: Meggs v Liverpool Corporation [1968] 1 All ER 1138
Mills v Barnsley Corporation [1999] PIQR 291

confidence.notes: Findings on defect, causation, and section 58 defence are explicit. Judge metadata lists Lord Denning historically but judgment is first-instance.

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused on solicitor negligence counterclaim by litigant in person
key_facts: Miss Evans sued former solicitors Clarke Willmott & Clarke for professional negligence in handling earlier building dispute litigation that ended in an adverse settlement costing her about £85,000.
She conducted a five-day trial in person and alleged inadequate pleading, failure to follow instructions, and an unfair trial.
The trial judge dismissed the counterclaim and ordered her to pay costs of about £97,000.
She sought permission to appeal both the merits decision and the costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal after trial of counterclaim for solicitor negligence.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal refused on both liability and costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant in person was given a fair trial and the trial judge properly controlled repetitive or irrelevant questioning, the Court of Appeal will not grant permission to appeal absent an arguable error of law; costs remain a matter for the trial judge's discretion and detailed assessment.
legal_issues: Whether the applicant received a fair trial as a litigant in person
Whether the judge erred in dismissing the professional negligence counterclaim
Whether the judge improperly exercised discretion on costs
Whether inadequate pleading by the solicitors was established

notes: Renewed sentence application after single judge refusal; totality and driving while disqualified points are concise.

enrichment.short_title: Totality sentence upheld for burglary and driving while disqualified
key_facts: The applicant pleaded guilty to burglary identified by DNA from blood at the scene and to driving while disqualified on a stolen moped.
He was on licence from a three-year sentence for earlier burglary and handling offences.
At Blackfriars Crown Court he received three months for licence breach, three years six months consecutive for burglary, and six months consecutive for driving while disqualified.
The total sentence was four years three months' imprisonment with a five-year driving disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence after refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; total sentence not held clearly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: Where an offender has a seriously poor record for repeated burglary and driving while disqualified and commits fresh offences on licence, a consecutive six-month sentence for driving while disqualified may be justified even without full credit for plea and even where it pushes total sentence above four years.
legal_issues: Whether the six-month consecutive sentence for driving while disqualified was manifestly excessive
Whether totality principles required reduction of the overall four years three months sentence
Whether credit for guilty pleas should have been given on the driving offence

enrichment.short_title: Second appeal refused on lease forfeiture and damages claim
key_facts: The tenant claimant was in rent arrears and the landlord changed the locks alleging abandonment of trade premises.
The tenant sought relief against forfeiture, damages, and exemplary damages; he was readmitted but the lease was terminated in February 2000.
District Judge Habershon dismissed the damages claim and awarded £15,490.66 on the counterclaim after a two-day trial.
Circuit Judge Behar allowed the appeal on forfeiture but dismissed appeals on damages and exemplary damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against a circuit judge's decision on a second appeal from county court proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: On a second appeal, the Court of Appeal will not intervene where disputed issues are questions of fact, including title to sue and quantum of counterclaim, and where exemplary damages were unavailable because the landlord's conduct was not calculated to make a profit within Rookes v Barnard.

Whether exemplary damages should have been awarded for unlawful forfeiture

notes: Defamation strike-out on limitation and costs adjournment appeal; detailed Limitation Act analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Defamation claim struck out on one-year limitation period
key_facts: Dr Hassan, an NHS SHO, sued consultants and his NHS trust over adverse GMC references given in 1997 that he said blighted his career.
He issued defamation proceedings in April 2003, outside the one-year section 4A primary limitation period from publication.
Mitting J struck out the defamation claim on limitation, concealment, discretion and related grounds; Poole J had adjourned an earlier strike-out hearing for late skeleton service.
A parallel breach of contract claim against the NHS trust continued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for permission to appeal against strike-out and a costs order for an adjourned hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications for permission to appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A defamation claim issued more than one year after the latest arguable publication is barred by section 4A Limitation Act 1980 unless deliberate concealment or a discretionary extension is established; mere retention of references on a confidential GMC file is not deliberate concealment, and section 35 does not automatically permit a time-barred defamation claim where section 32A discretion is refused.
legal_issues: Whether section 4A one-year limitation barred the defamation claim
Whether there was republication within the limitation period
Whether deliberate concealment under section 32(1)(b) applied
Whether section 32A or section 35 permitted the claim to proceed
Whether Poole J had jurisdiction to award costs for adjournment caused by late skeleton service
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank v Rogers [1996] EWCA Civ 1277

notes: TCC quantum meruit judgment on Sussex Stud redevelopment; lengthy valuation reasoning but outcome figure is stated.

enrichment.short_title: Quantum meruit claim for decorator works at Sussex Stud redevelopment

statutes_considered.title: Income Tax (Sub-contractors in the Construction Industry) Regulations 1993

key_facts: Mr Nash, trading as TJ Decorators, carried out decorating and building work on units 9–19 at The Sussex Stud residential redevelopment in Sussex.
Budget price letters in August 2001 and Fryatt's September 2001 acceptance letter did not form a binding contract because negotiations remained incomplete.
Tonbridge Estates paid £330,854 but disputed the balance claimed; expert surveyors largely agreed measured items.
The defendant raised set-offs for snagging, CIS tax deductions, VAT and delay costs, most of which failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court of claim for unpaid building works.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Mr Nash in the sum of £76,523.50 exclusive of interest on a quantum meruit basis; CIS and VAT set-off defences rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Where pre-contract budget correspondence and a purported acceptance letter leave key terms including programme unresolved, no binding construction contract is formed and the builder's entitlement falls to be assessed on quantum meruit for work done; absent contractual completion dates, delay-based management and interest set-offs fail, and failure to deduct CIS tax does not justify restitution where the builder has declared and paid tax on the income.
legal_issues: Whether a contract was concluded from August budget prices and the 22 September 2001 letter
The value of disputed and extra works on quantum meruit
Whether incomplete or defective work justified set-off
Whether the defendant could recover for failure to deduct CIS tax and VAT
Whether trade discounts and other Tonbridge Estates costs should be deducted
